narrative:
The model predicted a 96% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess academic readiness, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, followed by your LSAT score, then your first-year class ranking. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your first-year and third-year grades placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly sixth and fifth decile, respectively, among students who were accepted. These unusually low academic standings signaled to the model a high risk of struggling with the bar exam. Your LSAT score of 24 was also well below the average of 37 among accepted students, further increasing the predicted likelihood of failure. No other factors, including your middle family income, undergraduate GPA of 2.6, gender, race, or full-time study plans, played a meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Consider targeted test preparation or additional coursework before reapplying.
